title: Mortality-reducing detection of lethal cancers while they are still localized

concept.text: The innovation would be a screening assay and clinical pathway that find clinically consequential cancers while they remain confined and potentially curable, predict the organ of origin, and ultimately reduce cancer deaths. It would need to work in people without symptoms, with a false-positive burden acceptable for a healthy population. The broad ambition is to cover cancers responsible for a large share of deaths; evidence from a restricted cancer set would establish only that narrower scope.

Blood-based multi-cancer detection already demonstrates parts of this pathway: detecting a cancer signal and predicting where diagnostic investigation should begin. The proposed advance would connect those capabilities to timely treatment and demonstrated mortality reduction. The supplied NHS-Galleri reports establish detection and organ prediction, but do not establish this complete mortality-reducing capability.

significance.text: The supplied SEER statistics illustrate the burden of advanced diagnosis in two major lethal cancers. In the 2016–2022 data, 51% of lung cancers and 51% of pancreatic cancers were distant at diagnosis. Five-year relative survival was 65.5% for localized lung cancer versus 10.5% for distant disease, and 43.6% for localized pancreatic cancer versus 3.4% for distant disease. These figures motivate finding disease earlier, but they do not establish that most patients with every common lethal cancer are diagnosed after spread.

A Nature Communications study published on 19 February 2024 examined 1,030,937 people newly diagnosed with metastatic cancer in SEER during 1992–2019 and reported median survival of 10 months. Its Results report 833,535 deaths during follow-up, including 688,529 attributed to the originally diagnosed cancer: 82.6% of deaths. That denominator matters; the percentage does not describe all enrolled patients. The Discussion contains inconsistent percentages, while the explicit Results counts support this calculation. Cause-of-death misclassification and unequal follow-up also limit interpretation.

Conditional impact synthesis: a routine screening program that finds dangerous cancers while truly confined, directs workup accurately, and enables effective treatment could increase opportunities for cure across a population. Surgery or radiotherapy could contribute where local treatment is sufficient. The stage-survival associations above do not quantify additional cures caused by screening, establish that existing local treatments alone would suffice, or predict a particular mortality reduction.

The impact would depend on biological and clinical limits as well as assay accuracy. Earlier diagnosis cannot by itself eliminate microscopic dissemination, make an ineffective treatment curative, or determine whether a detected lesion would ever become lethal. The research specifically raises occult spread in apparently localized pancreatic cancer, but the supplied reviewed evidence does not directly substantiate that disease-specific assertion. It remains a qualified concern rather than an established finding in this record. Likewise, no historical proposal of sensitivity and specificity above 95%, or mortality reduction above 50%, is adopted as an evidence-based expectation.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability within the supplied evidence is reliable detection of consequential disease early enough to change outcomes, combined with organ prediction and a safe route to diagnosis and treatment. The NHS-Galleri performance report documents incomplete episode sensitivity despite high specificity and organ-prediction accuracy. Its results illustrate why a positive signal and a plausible origin do not by themselves establish detection of localized lethal disease or clinical benefit.

Proposed biological barriers from the research include very small amounts of tumor-derived DNA, proteins, or cells in blood early in disease, and signals that may overlap with clonal hematopoiesis, inflammation, or indolent lesions. These are concrete candidate explanations for the difficulty of the task, but the supplied reviewed sources do not verify them. Their importance, relative contribution, and relevance to particular assay designs remain unresolved here.

Engineering synthesis: the assay must balance missed cancers against false alarms while retaining enough information to guide an organ-specific investigation. The clinical pathway must then resolve positive results without an excessive burden of invasive procedures in people without cancer. A further challenge is determining which detected lesions need intervention and whether apparently confined disease is treatable with curative intent. These requirements connect measurement, diagnostic workup, tumor biology, and treatment; improving any single component would not automatically solve the whole task.

The clinical validation barrier is demonstrating fewer deaths after introducing screening. A decrease in late-stage diagnoses could support the proposed mechanism, but it would not alone fulfill this concept's mortality-based goal. The supplied randomized trial used a stage-based primary endpoint, leaving the stronger mortality question unanswered by its reported primary analysis.

current_state.text: The research attributes a 2021 targeted-methylation case-control validation to Klein and colleagues in Annals of Oncology, reporting specificity of 99.5%, overall sensitivity of 51.5%, stage I sensitivity of 16.8% with a 95% confidence interval of 14.5–19.5%, and stage IV sensitivity of 90.1%. These figures are retained as unresolved reported values: the review found that the saved artifact for the cited PubMed URL contained only a cookie error, with no article identity or results available for verification. That access failure does not show that the figures are false. Even if confirmed, a case-control validation would not itself demonstrate population screening mortality benefit.

The supplied abstract of the NHS-Galleri randomized trial, attributed to Sasieni and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine on 8 October 2026, reports assignment of 71,122 people aged 50–77 to testing and 71,128 to a control group with stored blood. After three screening rounds and at least 12 months of follow-up after the last participant's third visit, the incidence rate ratio for stage III or IV disease across 12 prespecified cancer types was 1.03, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.92–1.14 and P=0.63. The trial therefore did not demonstrate a reduction in its combined late-stage primary endpoint.

The same trial abstract reports a stage IV incidence rate ratio of 0.86, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.74–1.00. This separate result does not replace the combined stage III-or-IV primary result or establish fewer cancer deaths. Conversely, the nonsignificant primary result does not establish equivalence between groups or exclude a mortality benefit emerging with further follow-up. Mortality was not the endpoint of the reported primary analysis.

The companion NHS-Galleri performance report, attributed to Neal and colleagues in Nature Medicine on 22 September 2026, reports descriptive secondary analyses in evaluable intervention participants. Across screening rounds, episode sensitivity ranged from 26.7% to 37.2% for all cancers and from 47.6% to 63.4% for the 12 prespecified cancer types. Specificity ranged from 99.50% to 99.60%, and cancer-signal-origin accuracy ranged from 91.1% to 93.6%. Referrals were informed by the predicted origin.

Cancer-signal-origin accuracy describes localization following detection; it is not stage I sensitivity. The exact denominator and supplementary definitions for that accuracy measure require the full methods. The reviewed abstracts establish that the test detects some cancers and often predicts a likely origin, but do not establish that most detected cancers were later-stage. Higher sensitivity in advanced disease, even if the earlier validation figures are confirmed, would not by itself establish the stage distribution of detected cases.

The supplied review's assessment of the two 2026 reports is limited to identified abstracts; full trial methods, figures, and supplementary definitions were not inspected. A NORC PDF retained under the trial source is a different document and supplies no validation of these trial results. The supplied freshness record also contains no bounded search entries, so comprehensive coverage of the field through 1 November 2026 is unresolved. The documented results stand within their dated scope, without establishing either achievement or universal absence of the proposed capability across the field.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed convincing demonstration: a randomized population trial should show that adding the screening program to usual care reduces cancer mortality for a prespecified set of lethal cancers lacking effective screening. The population, cancer set, screening schedule, mortality endpoint, follow-up duration, and analysis should be specified in advance. A fall in late-stage diagnoses would support the intended pathway, but would not meet this mortality-based criterion unless deaths also fall. This is a proposed evaluation standard for this concept, not an established authoritative threshold.
completion_criteria.label: Randomized screening reduces mortality from prespecified lethal cancers

completion_criteria.text: Proposed diagnostic and harm criteria: organ prediction should be accurate enough to direct useful workup, and the program should meet prespecified limits on invasive procedures in people who do not have cancer. Evaluation should report sensitivity by cancer type and stage, specificity, organ-prediction accuracy with explicit denominators, and the outcomes of positive-result investigations. Numerical acceptance thresholds should be justified for the intended population rather than inherited from the unverified historical proposals.
completion_criteria.label: Organ-directed workup meets prespecified invasive-procedure limits for cancer-free people

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: the assay and diagnostic pathway should produce consistent results across independent sites and relevant participant groups, with confirmatory evaluation sufficient to show that the mortality benefit and harm balance are not confined to one setting. Practical assessment should establish whether workup and treatment can be delivered reliably at the tested scale. Success would establish demonstrated breadth for the studied populations, cancer types, and follow-up period; finite trials would not prove coverage of all cancers or automatically establish the broader ambition of covering cancers responsible for most deaths.
completion_criteria.label: Mortality benefit and harm balance reproduce across independent settings

related_concepts.text: Roster-based comparison: ONC-10, “A reliable distinction between early neoplasms that will kill and those that will not,” is the closest conceptual overlap. ONC-01 concerns finding consequential cancers early enough to reduce mortality; ONC-10 concerns predicting which early lesions warrant treatment. Better discrimination could help ONC-01 avoid unnecessary intervention, but detecting a signal or predicting its organ does not establish a lesion's future lethality. Only ONC-10's title and the candidate's brief description are supplied, so a fuller scope comparison remains unavailable.

Roster-based comparison: ONC-08, “Interception of non-viral precancers before they invade,” and ONC-09, “Prophylactic immunity that prevents the common non-viral cancers,” act earlier in disease development. ONC-08 targets precancers, while ONC-09 seeks prevention through immunity. ONC-01 seeks mortality reduction by detecting existing cancer while localized. The approaches could complement one another, but prevention, precancer interception, and cancer screening remain distinct capabilities.

Roster-based comparison: ONC-02, “Sterilizing immune clearance of established metastatic carcinomas,” addresses disease after spread, whereas ONC-03, “Eradication of dormant disseminated tumor cells that cause late relapse,” targets disseminated cells associated with later recurrence. Both are relevant to the limits of earlier diagnosis: successful screening would not itself clear established metastases or eradicate dormant disseminated cells.

Roster-based comparison: ONC-04, “A shared malignant dependency that renewing normal tissues can spare,” ONC-05, “Therapies that drive the whole clonal population to extinction,” and ONC-06, “Stable reversion of carcinoma cells to non-malignant tissue identity,” describe different treatment ambitions. ONC-07, “Body-wide delivery that alters essentially every malignant cell,” addresses therapeutic reach. These could expand the treatment options available after diagnosis, but ONC-01 neither demonstrates nor requires achievement of those particular therapeutic mechanisms.

Roster-based comparison: ONC-11, “Real-time, cell-resolution guidance that makes incomplete cancer surgery uncommon,” could complement earlier detection by improving local treatment completeness; it does not provide population screening or prove a screening mortality benefit. ONC-12, “Off-the-shelf cell therapy that matches autologous cures and can be given at ordinary scale,” concerns treatment efficacy and delivery at scale. It could broaden treatment access after diagnosis, while remaining separate from detection and organ prediction. These comparisons are limited to the supplied roster titles.

unresolved_issues: The 2021 validation's document identity and reported performance figures remain unverified because the retained artifact contains only a cookie error. The review's recommendation to remove reliance on these figures was adopted, but its omission of the numbers was not: they are preserved solely as unresolved reported values.
The supplied evidence does not verify the low-shedding and overlapping-signal mechanisms or the pancreas-specific occult-dissemination assertion.
The exact denominator, definitions, and subgroup methods for cancer-signal-origin accuracy require full-methods assessment; the supplied review inspected abstracts only.
Mortality outcomes and longer-term follow-up are not established by the supplied trial reports.

The metastatic study's inconsistent Discussion percentages remain unreconciled, although its Results counts support the qualified 82.6% figure. Supplements and figure images were not inspected in the supplied review, including a listed supplement with little extractable text.
No supplied bounded freshness search establishes comprehensive coverage through 1 November 2026 or field-wide absence of the proposed capability.

The population, cancer coverage, mortality endpoint, follow-up duration, acceptable diagnostic harms, reproducibility requirements, and practical delivery limits for a definitive demonstration still require specification.
Full records for the related concepts were not supplied; their relationships are therefore limited to the roster titles and the brief ONC-10 description.

brief.title: Finding deadly cancers early enough to save lives
possible: People without symptoms could have a screening test that finds dangerous cancers before they spread and tells doctors which organ to investigate. A linked route through diagnosis and treatment would catch disease while cure is still possible and reduce cancer deaths.
why: Lung and pancreatic cancers are often diagnosed after they have spread. Finding dangerous cancers while they remain confined could give more people a chance of cure, including through surgery or radiotherapy when treatment of the original site is sufficient.

sources.showed: Lung cancer survival is much higher when the disease is confined to its original site than when it has spread to distant parts of the body.
sources.quote: The earlier lung and bronchus cancer is caught, the better chance a person has of surviving five years after being diagnosed.
sources.cited_for: Lung cancer outcomes differ sharply according to how far the disease has spread at diagnosis.
sources.not_established: Survival differences do not establish how many deaths screening would prevent.

sources.showed: Pancreatic cancer is often diagnosed after distant spread, when survival is much poorer than for disease confined to the pancreas.
sources.quote: The earlier pancreatic cancer is caught, the better chance a person has of surviving five years after being diagnosed.
sources.cited_for: Pancreatic cancer illustrates the need to find dangerous disease before it spreads.
sources.not_established: These statistics do not show that screening would make more pancreatic cancers curable.

sources.showed: Among people newly diagnosed with cancer that had spread to distant sites, most deaths during follow-up were attributed to the original cancer.
sources.quote: The median survival time among all metastatic cancer patients is 10 months
sources.cited_for: Cancer that has spread can carry a heavy burden of early death.
sources.not_established: This observational study did not test whether screening prevents cancer deaths.

sources.showed: A blood test detected signals from many cancer types and often identified their organ of origin. It missed most cancers at the earliest stage in a study comparing people with and without cancer.
sources.quote: Cancer signals were detected across >50 cancer types.
sources.cited_for: Blood testing can detect multiple cancer types, but early disease remains difficult to find.
sources.not_established: A comparison of people with and without cancer does not establish benefit from routine screening.

sources.showed: The NHS-Galleri randomized trial did not demonstrate fewer late-stage diagnoses on its main measure when blood testing was added to usual care.
sources.quote: Less than 1% of participants had trial-related adverse events; none were serious.
sources.cited_for: A large screening trial has tested the pathway without demonstrating its intended reduction in late-stage diagnoses.
sources.not_established: The reported analysis does not establish fewer cancer deaths or rule out a benefit with longer follow-up.

sources.showed: The test for early detection of multiple cancers (MCED) found some cancers and usually predicted their organ of origin. Many cancers went undetected.
sources.quote: In aggregate, 937 participants had MCED-detected primary cancers.
sources.cited_for: Population screening can detect cancer signals and guide doctors toward an organ to investigate.
sources.not_established: Predicting the organ of origin does not establish that a cancer is still confined or that finding it saves a life.

shown: The NHS-Galleri researchers have shown that a blood test can find some cancers in people without symptoms and often point doctors toward the right organ. Their randomized trial did not demonstrate a reduction in its main measure of late-stage cancer diagnoses.
missing: Screening still needs to reliably find cancers that would become lethal while they remain confined and treatable.
Positive results need a dependable route to diagnosis and treatment, with acceptable limits on invasive procedures in people without cancer.
A randomized trial still needs to demonstrate fewer cancer deaths from adding the screening program to usual care.
Independent settings need to reproduce the balance of lives saved and harms caused.

milestones.label: Screening reduces deaths from specified lethal cancers
milestones.explanation: A trial assigning people at random would have to show fewer deaths from cancers chosen in advance that lack effective screening. This would establish that the program saves lives.

milestones.label: Organ prediction guides diagnosis within invasive procedure limits
milestones.explanation: The program would have to guide useful organ-specific investigations and meet advance limits on invasive procedures in cancer-free people. This would establish an acceptable burden from investigating positive results.

milestones.label: Benefits and harms hold across independent settings
milestones.explanation: Independent sites and relevant participant groups would have to reproduce the mortality benefit and harm balance, with reliable diagnosis and treatment at the tested scale. This would establish where the program works in practice.

uncertain: It remains unclear which detected cancers need treatment and whether apparently confined disease is still curable.
Longer follow-up could change the trial's findings; its effect on cancer deaths remains unknown.
Acceptable limits on diagnostic harms and the cancer types and populations covered by a definitive trial still need to be set.

page.title: Multi-cancer early detection with reduced cancer mortality
page.definition: A multi-cancer screening programme uses one test to look for signs of several cancers in people without symptoms. A positive result prompts diagnostic investigation, sometimes guided by a prediction of the organ or tissue of origin. The goal is to reduce deaths from the cancers being sought by adding this pathway and treatment of confirmed cancers to usual care, including existing screening.

goal.need: In 2018–2019, 60.1% of the 1,198,854 US cancer deaths came from cancer types outside the four with a grade A or B screening recommendation. Even full uptake of breast, cervical, colorectal and lung screening would leave that gap. Testing for several cancers in one sample could give people with other cancers a chance to receive effective treatment before symptoms appear. The benefit must outweigh harms from unnecessary investigations and treatment of cancers that would never have caused illness.

completion.title: Multi-cancer screening reduces cancer mortality in randomized controlled trials.
completion.criterion: Adequately powered, high-quality randomised trials show that people offered multi-cancer screening in addition to usual care have a lower death rate from the target cancers than people offered usual care alone. Both groups retain access to established screening. The benefits of the full programme, including diagnostic investigation and treatment, outweigh its harms. The finding applies to the populations, cancers, screening schedules and follow-up studied.
completion.set_by: UK National Screening Committee, population screening criteria 11 and 13 and 2026 position statements on multicancer detection tests and surrogate outcomes.
completion.threshold_quote: There should be evidence from high quality randomised controlled trials that the screening programme is effective in reducing mortality or morbidity.
completion.basis: Cancer mortality is the phase 5 outcome in the EDRN framework. The UK National Screening Committee treats late-stage incidence as an intermediate outcome. Across 12 prespecified cancer types, NHS-Galleri reported a stage III or IV incidence rate ratio of 1.03 after three screening rounds (95% CI 0.92 to 1.14, P = 0.63). The stage IV comparison was descriptive. The trial was not powered to establish a mortality reduction.

milestones.title: Laboratory comparisons identify cancer-associated biomarkers in tumour and noncancer specimens.
milestones.criterion: A comparison of tumour and noncancer specimens identifies measurable differences that could serve as markers of cancer in a screening assay.

milestones.threshold_quote: To identify leads for potentially useful biomarkers.

milestones.title: A multi-cancer assay distinguishes diagnosed cancer cases from noncancer controls.
milestones.criterion: In specimens from people with clinically diagnosed cancer and controls without cancer, the assay distinguishes the two groups. Estimate the proportions testing positive in each group at the chosen cutoff, or across a range of cutoffs.
milestones.set_by: NCI Early Detection Research Network’s five-phase framework, phase 2, described by Pepe and colleagues.
milestones.threshold_quote: distinguish subjects with cancer from those without cancer

milestones.title: A multi-cancer assay detects cancer in specimens collected before clinical diagnosis.
milestones.criterion: Use stored specimens from a cohort followed for cancer diagnoses. Compare specimens collected before diagnosis from people who later developed cancer with specimens from controls in the same cohort. Determine how far before clinical diagnosis the assay can distinguish the groups and define a positive test for prospective screening.
milestones.set_by: NCI Early Detection Research Network’s five-phase framework, phase 3, described by Pepe and colleagues.
milestones.threshold_quote: To evaluate, as a function of time before clinical diagnosis, the capacity of the biomarker to detect preclinical disease.

milestones.title: Prospective multi-cancer screening measures cancer detection and false-referral rates.
milestones.criterion: Screen people prospectively and investigate positive results. Among all people screened, estimate the proportion who test positive and have cancer confirmed and the proportion referred after a positive test who do not have cancer. Describe the types and stages of the cancers detected.
milestones.set_by: NCI Early Detection Research Network, Third Report, March 2005, Figure 1, phase 4.
milestones.threshold_quote: Identify the extent and characteristics of disease detected by the test and determine the false referral rate

milestones.title: Screening significantly reduces stage III or IV incidence across 12 prespecified cancer types.
milestones.criterion: Under the NHS-Galleri protocol, compare three annual rounds of multi-cancer testing plus usual care with usual care alone. From randomisation through at least 12 months after the last participant’s third visit, the rate of first eligible stage III or IV diagnoses per person-year must be lower in the intervention arm for the 12 prespecified cancer types combined (two-sided P < 0.05). This is a trial-specific intermediate endpoint.
milestones.set_by: NHS-Galleri randomised trial protocol, ISRCTN91431511, primary endpoint and prespecified testing order.
milestones.threshold_quote: a statistically significant reduction in the incidence rate of stage III and IV cancers diagnosed in the intervention versus control arm

not_found: NCI EDRN and UK NSC documents did not supply universal numerical accuracy or diagnostic-harm acceptance limits.
No published randomized multi-cancer screening result demonstrating reduced cancer mortality was located.

results.finding: NHS-Galleri (142,250 randomized) reported a stage III or IV cancer incidence rate ratio of 1.03 across the 12 prespecified cancer types.
results.detail: The stage IV-only secondary endpoint had an incidence rate ratio of 0.86 (95% CI, 0.74 to 1.00). The milestone is based on the combined stage III or IV primary endpoint.
results.quote: The incidence rate of stage III or IV cancer (primary end point) did not differ significantly between the groups (incidence rate ratio [intervention vs. control], 1.03; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.92 to 1.14, P = 0.63).

results.finding: The targeted methylation assay had 51.5% sensitivity in an independent case-control validation of 4,077 participants.
results.detail: Controls had their noncancer status confirmed at one-year follow-up.

results.finding: Among 303 NHS-Galleri participants with a first-round false positive, 17.8% were diagnosed with cancer in later rounds.
results.detail: The post hoc analysis used annual follow-up windows. It gives the frequency of later diagnosis among initially false-positive participants.
results.quote: In a post hoc analysis of participants with results classified as false positive in the first round, 17.8% (54/303) were subsequently diagnosed with cancer during the second or third round follow-up windows, including 36 cases in the second round and 18 cases in the third round

results.finding: Galleri detected primary cancer in 0.48% of 197,146 evaluable NHS-Galleri screens over three annual rounds.
results.detail: The denominator counts screening tests across rounds and includes repeat participants. The primary analysis used up to 12 months of follow-up per round. An exploratory review identified 36 recurrences among the 864 positive referrals without a confirmed primary cancer.
results.quote: In aggregate, 937 participants had MCED-detected primary cancers.

results.finding: PanSeer identified 477 differentially methylated regions across 200 tumour and noncancer specimens.
results.quote: We processed these samples using the PanSeer assay and identified a set of 477 differentially methylated regions (DMRs, see “Methods” section).

results.finding: PanSeer tested positive in 87.6% of 113 diagnosed cancer cases, compared with 207 noncancer controls.
results.quote: We show that PanSeer detects five common types of cancer in 88% (95% CI: 80–93%) of post-diagnosis patients with a specificity of 96% (95% CI: 93–98%),

results.finding: PanSeer detected 94.9% of 98 prediagnosis cases in a held-out comparison with 207 same-cohort controls.
results.detail: The analysis was retrospective. Table 1 and Methods give 98 held-out prediagnosis cases. One Results sentence gives 143.
results.quote: We also demonstrate that PanSeer detects cancer in 95% (95% CI: 89–98%) of asymptomatic individuals who were later diagnosed, though future longitudinal studies are required to confirm this result.

results.finding: The plasma 3p copy-number signal differed between 178 late-stage lung cancer cases and 2,655 normal controls (P = 3.33 × 10⁻¹⁶).
results.quote: The 2 sample ks-test with mean Copyome value for the given band between normal and NSCLC samples showed a p-value of 3.33e-16 (KS test statistic: 0.39) for 3p, 5.37e-9 (KS test statistic: 0.24) for 3q26-29, and 6.68e-7 (KS test statistic: 0.21) for 6q25-24.

results.finding: ABCDai-MCED achieved 99.6% specificity in a holdout set of 526 diagnosed cancer cases and 2,149 controls.
results.quote:
ABCDai-MCED’s performance on the stratification of blood samples from the independent cohort of patients with cancer versus those with no reported cancer resulted in sensitivities for stages I-IV (
n
= 284, 129, 90, and 23, respectively) of 83.1%, 86.0%, 84.4%, and 95.7% at 99.6% specificity (
n
= 2149).

results.finding: MethylScan identified 15,155 candidate methylation markers from 189 matched tumour–normal tissue pairs.
results.detail: The authors also checked whether the markers distinguished tumour from normal tissue using independent TCGA methylation array data.
results.quote: The final marker set combines these identified regions from all cancer types, totaling 15,155 markers ( Dataset S3 ).

results.finding: MethylScan achieved 63.3% sensitivity in a plasma study of 861 participants.
results.detail: Estimates came from 50 repeats of stratified fivefold cross-validation. Plasma donors were distinct from the tissue donors used to discover the markers.
results.quote: We achieved an average area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.938 (95% CI: 0.920 to 0.954) with a sensitivity of 63.3% (95% CI: 58.9 to 67.9%) at 98.0% specificity in the fivefold cross validations ( Fig. 6 C ).

results.finding: In 2,754 CPS-3 participants, the methylation assay detected 2.3% of cancers three years before clinical diagnosis.
results.detail: The study used one blood draw per participant and applied the previously validated classifier without retraining.
results.quote: Among all cancers, detectability was 15.2%, 6.0%, and 2.3% for samples collected 1, 2, and 3 year(s) before diagnosis, respectively.

results.finding: Comparison of 197 tumour and normal tissue specimens identified 115,220 hypomethylated pan-cancer regions.
results.detail: The study reanalysed previously published sequencing data. The authors defined pan-cancer regions by consistent methylation changes in at least six cancer types.
results.quote: Across the genome, we identified 5,398 hypermethylated and 115,220 hypomethylated pan-cancer DMRs

results.finding: Six multi-cancer assays evaluated across 549 cancer cases and 413 controls had a median case positivity of 52.1% at their own cutoffs.
results.detail: Performance was summarized across assays. The 549 cases and 413 controls make up the reference set assessed by at least one assay, and the mix of cancer types varied by assay.

results.finding: PATHFINDER 2 found a 0.54% cancer detection rate with Galleri among 32,007 screened adults with complete 12-month follow-up.
results.detail: The 42.4% is calculated from the diagnostic workup cohort. Of the 123 with no cancer diagnosis, 108 reached diagnostic resolution and 15 had unresolved workups.
results.quote:
Of these, 173 had true-positive test results, 
for a cancer detection rate of 0.54%

definition = "A multi-cancer screening programme uses one test to look for signs of several cancers in people without symptoms. A positive result prompts diagnostic investigation, sometimes guided by a prediction of the organ or tissue of origin. The goal is to reduce deaths from the cancers being sought by adding this pathway and treatment of confirmed cancers to usual care, including existing screening.". Reason: The current definition makes localisation a requirement and leaves unclear how a screening signal leads to a confirmed diagnosis.

goal.need = "In 2018\u20132019, 60.1% of the 1,198,854 US cancer deaths came from cancer types outside the four with a grade A or B screening recommendation. Even full uptake of breast, cervical, colorectal and lung screening would leave that gap. Testing for several cancers in one sample could give people with other cancers a chance to receive effective treatment before symptoms appear. The benefit must outweigh harms from unnecessary investigations and treatment of cancers that would never have caused illness.". Reason: The lung survival figures describe prognosis within one cancer type but leave out the size of the screening gap and how closing it could benefit patients.

add statement by Department of Health and Social Care and NHS England, 2026: "multi-cancer early detection tests can become part of our national screening programmes". Reason: England’s 2026 cancer plan adds an explicit, conditional goal for national screening to the existing statements about evaluating tests.

edit completion: criterion = "Adequately powered, high-quality randomised trials show that people offered multi-cancer screening in addition to usual care have a lower death rate from the target cancers than people offered usual care alone. Both groups retain access to established screening. The benefits of the full programme, including diagnostic investigation and treatment, outweigh its harms. The finding applies to the populations, cancers, screening schedules and follow-up studied."; set_by = "UK National Screening Committee, population screening criteria 11 and 13 and 2026 position statements on multicancer detection tests and surrogate outcomes."; threshold_quote = "There should be evidence from high quality randomised controlled trials that the screening programme is effective in reducing mortality or morbidity."; threshold_ref = 5; basis = "Cancer mortality is the phase 5 outcome in the EDRN framework. The UK National Screening Committee treats late-stage incidence as an intermediate outcome. Across 12 prespecified cancer types, NHS-Galleri reported a stage III or IV incidence rate ratio of 1.03 after three screening rounds (95% CI 0.92 to 1.14, P = 0.63). The stage IV comparison was descriptive. The trial was not powered to establish a mortality reduction."; refs = [5, 6, 15, 19, 14]. Reason: The 2026 committee statements specify the target-cancer mortality comparison, and the primary NHS-Galleri report gives the randomised result directly.

edit m1: criterion = "A comparison of tumour and noncancer specimens identifies measurable differences that could serve as markers of cancer in a screening assay.". Reason: The PanSeer tissue counts and discovery result belong with the evidence for phase 1, while the criterion should state what a laboratory comparison must show.

edit m2: criterion = "In specimens from people with clinically diagnosed cancer and controls without cancer, the assay distinguishes the two groups. Estimate the proportions testing positive in each group at the chosen cutoff, or across a range of cutoffs.". Reason: The current criterion mixes CCGA’s observed percentages with the EDRN test of whether an assay distinguishes diagnosed cases from controls.

edit m3: criterion = "Use stored specimens from a cohort followed for cancer diagnoses. Compare specimens collected before diagnosis from people who later developed cancer with specimens from controls in the same cohort. Determine how far before clinical diagnosis the assay can distinguish the groups and define a positive test for prospective screening."; threshold_quote = "To evaluate, as a function of time before clinical diagnosis, the capacity of the biomarker to detect preclinical disease."; threshold_ref = 6. Reason: EDRN phase 3 measures detection as a function of time before diagnosis, whereas the current criterion gives one study’s four-year window and accuracy estimates.

edit m4: title = "Prospective multi-cancer screening measures cancer detection and false-referral rates."; criterion = "Screen people prospectively and investigate positive results. Among all people screened, estimate the proportion who test positive and have cancer confirmed and the proportion referred after a positive test who do not have cancer. Describe the types and stages of the cancers detected."; refs = [6, 7, 10]. Reason: The current title omits false referrals, and the trial counts in the criterion obscure the denominator for both phase 4 rates.

add milestone after m4: "Screening significantly reduces stage III or IV incidence across 12 prespecified cancer types.". Reason: The NHS-Galleri protocol supplies a randomised intermediate test between measuring diagnostic yield and determining whether screening prevents cancer deaths.
remove not found 2. Reason: The full NHS-Galleri primary report and both May 2026 UK National Screening Committee position statements are available in full text.
